case_info.scenario: A 57-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 5 months of epigastric pain and a 6.8-kg (15-lb) weight loss. He had no fevers or night sweats. Physical examination was notable for oral thrush and mild epigastric tenderness. Results of a fourth-generation HIV Ab/Ag combination assay were positive, and subsequent testing showed a CD4 cell count of 16/mm3and an HIV viral load greater than 10 million copies/mL. Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis showed thickening of the walls of the stomach, duodenum, and colon as well as multiple masses in the right hepatic lobe measuring up to 6.9 cm in diameter. A core biopsy of one of the liver masses demonstrated diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. He started antiretroviral therapy with bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir/alafenamide and chemotherapy with rituximab, etoposide, prednisone, vincristine, cyclophosphamide, and doxorubicin (R-EPOCH). Four weeks after initiation of chemotherapy, the patient developed sudden onset of bright red blood per rectum, tachycardia, and hypotension. Mesenteric computed tomography angiography demonstrated active extravasation in the jejunum from a branch of the superior mesenteric artery. After unsuccessful coil embolization, he underwent open resection of 40 cm of distal small intestine; pathological examination of a stained section showed acute inflammation of the lamina propria, with crypt epithelial apoptosis and numerous cytoplasmic and nuclear inclusions with an “owl eye” appearance (Figure 1, left panel). Five weeks later, he developed blurred vision, and visual acuity testing revealed 20/50 vision in the left eye and 20/70 in the right eye. A dilated retinal examination revealed extensive macular hemorrhage in the left eye, with peripapillary whitening and perivascular hemorrhage with whitening along the superior vascular arcade (Figure, right panel).

case_info.explanation: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis and hemorrhagic enteritis The keys to the correct diagnosis in this case are the patient’s blurred vision and gastrointestinal hemorrhage in the setting of a profound immunocompromised state. This should prompt consideration of opportunistic infectious pathogens with tropisms for the eye and gastrointestinal tract, such asToxoplasma, CMV, andCandida. The histopathologic finding of acute inflammation of the lamina propria with cytoplasmic and nuclear inclusions surrounded by a clear halo (“owl eye” sign) (Figure, left panel) confirms the diagnosis of CMV enteritis (choice C). While herpes simplex virus (choice A) is a common opportunistic infection with both ocular and gastrointestinal manifestations, it typically causes a painful keratitis and rarely involves the small or large intestines.1Vitreous fluid sampling (choice B) is occasionally indicated to evaluate for ocular involvement of lymphoma, but this procedure has associated risks and should be preceded by a thorough dilated eye examination. While Crohn disease (choice D) might present with both ocular and gastrointestinal manifestations, the patient’s age, immunocompromised state, and acute presentation make opportunistic infections more likely. Cytomegalovirus is a double-stranded DNA virus of the Herpesvirus family that typically remains latent in a host after acute infection.2CMV is rarely a cause of severe disease in immunocompetent individuals. However, in immunocompromised patients such as HIV-infected patients and solid organ or hematopoietic transplant recipients, CMV can cause life-threatening, tissue-invasive disease.1,3,4In the era of antiretroviral therapy, the incidence of tissue-invasive CMV in patients with HIV is 1.2 per 1000 person-years; however, the incidence in patients with CD4 cell counts 50/mm3or less is 39 per 1000 person-years.5The most common sites of end-organ disease in HIV-infected individuals are the gastrointestinal tract (1.3 per 1000 person years) and eye (2 per 1000 person years).5In solid organ and allogeneic stem cell transplant recipients, the risk of tissue-invasive CMV infection is 3% to 10% and most frequently involves the lungs (4%) and the gastrointestinal tract (3%).4,6 CMV can affect any portion of the gastrointestinal tract but typically involves the esophagus and colon, which account for 15% and 57% of gastrointestinal tract involvement in immunocompromised hosts, respectively.7Patients with ileocolic infection may present with abdominal pain, chronic diarrhea, gastrointestinal bleeding, and perforation.7The diagnosis of tissue-invasive CMV infection requires histopathologic confirmation. Neither blood antigen testing nor whole-blood DNA polymerase chain reaction assay is sufficiently sensitive or specific to reliably diagnose CMV gastrointestinal tract disease.8 All patients with invasive CMV disease should undergo a dilated ophthalmic examination to evaluate for concomitant CMV retinitis. On ophthalmoscopic examination, CMV presents as confluent areas of retinal necrosis with hemorrhages beginning in the posterior pole and spreading centripetally. Intravenous ganciclovir is a common first-line agent to treat CMV colitis or esophagitis. If there are no concerns about intestinal absorption, oral valganciclovir is an effective alternative, based on its excellent bioavailability and noninferiority to intravenous ganciclovir in a randomized clinical trial.9Duration of therapy is 21 to 42 days or until signs and symptoms have resolved. For CMV retinitis, either intravenous ganciclovir or oral valganciclovir should be administered during an induction period lasting 14 to 21 days, with the duration determined by clinical response based on retinal examination. Induction should be followed by oral maintenance therapy with valganciclovir lasting 3 to 6 months or until immune reconstitution.1 After resection of the small intestine, the patient was treated with oral valganciclovir for 3 weeks, with no recurrence in gastrointestinal bleeding. A dilated eye examination demonstrated findings consistent with CMV retinitis, and he completed 14 days of intravenous ganciclovir followed by maintenance oral valganciclovir, with improvement in his vision. After 6 cycles of dose-adjusted R-EPOCH, a positron emission tomography scan demonstrated a complete response. He continued to receive antiretroviral therapy and had a CD4 cell count of 337/mm3at the time of last follow-up.

       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:

       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis and hemorrhagic enteritis The keys to the correct diagnosis in this case are the patient’s blurred vision and gastrointestinal hemorrhage in the setting of a profound immunocompromised state. This should prompt consideration of opportunistic infectious pathogens with tropisms for the eye and gastrointestinal tract, such asToxoplasma, CMV, andCandida. The histopathologic finding of acute inflammation of the lamina propria with cytoplasmic and nuclear inclusions surrounded by a clear halo (“owl eye” sign) (Figure, left panel) confirms the diagnosis of CMV enteritis (choice C). While herpes simplex virus (choice A) is a common opportunistic infection with both ocular and gastrointestinal manifestations, it typically causes a painful keratitis and rarely involves the small or large intestines.1Vitreous fluid sampling (choice B) is occasionally indicated to evaluate for ocular involvement of lymphoma, but this procedure has associated risks and should be preceded by a thorough dilated eye examination. While Crohn disease (choice D) might present with both ocular and gastrointestinal manifestations, the patient’s age, immunocompromised state, and acute presentation make opportunistic infections more likely. Cytomegalovirus is a double-stranded DNA virus of the Herpesvirus family that typically remains latent in a host after acute infection.2CMV is rarely a cause of severe disease in immunocompetent individuals. However, in immunocompromised patients such as HIV-infected patients and solid organ or hematopoietic transplant recipients, CMV can cause life-threatening, tissue-invasive disease.1,3,4In the era of antiretroviral therapy, the incidence of tissue-invasive CMV in patients with HIV is 1.2 per 1000 person-years; however, the incidence in patients with CD4 cell counts 50/mm3or less is 39 per 1000 person-years.5The most common sites of end-organ disease in HIV-infected individuals are the gastrointestinal tract (1.3 per 1000 person years) and eye (2 per 1000 person years).5In solid organ and allogeneic stem cell transplant recipients, the risk of tissue-invasive CMV infection is 3% to 10% and most frequently involves the lungs (4%) and the gastrointestinal tract (3%).4,6 CMV can affect any portion of the gastrointestinal tract but typically involves the esophagus and colon, which account for 15% and 57% of gastrointestinal tract involvement in immunocompromised hosts, respectively.7Patients with ileocolic infection may present with abdominal pain, chronic diarrhea, gastrointestinal bleeding, and perforation.7The diagnosis of tissue-invasive CMV infection requires histopathologic confirmation. Neither blood antigen testing nor whole-blood DNA polymerase chain reaction assay is sufficiently sensitive or specific to reliably diagnose CMV gastrointestinal tract disease.8 All patients with invasive CMV disease should undergo a dilated ophthalmic examination to evaluate for concomitant CMV retinitis. On ophthalmoscopic examination, CMV presents as confluent areas of retinal necrosis with hemorrhages beginning in the posterior pole and spreading centripetally. Intravenous ganciclovir is a common first-line agent to treat CMV colitis or esophagitis. case_info.explanation: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis and hemorrhagic enteritis The keys to the correct diagnosis in this case are the patient’s blurred vision and gastrointestinal hemorrhage in the setting of a profound immunocompromised state. This should prompt consideration of opportunistic infectious pathogens with tropisms for the eye and gastrointestinal tract, such asToxoplasma, CMV, andCandida. The histopathologic finding of acute inflammation of the lamina propria with cytoplasmic and nuclear inclusions surrounded by a clear halo (“owl eye” sign) (Figure, left panel) confirms the diagnosis of CMV enteritis (choice C). While herpes simplex virus (choice A) is a common opportunistic infection with both ocular and gastrointestinal manifestations, it typically causes a painful keratitis and rarely involves the small or large intestines.1Vitreous fluid sampling (choice B) is occasionally indicated to evaluate for ocular involvement of lymphoma, but this procedure has associated risks and should be preceded by a thorough dilated eye examination. While Crohn disease (choice D) might present with both ocular and gastrointestinal manifestations, the patient’s age, immunocompromised state, and acute presentation make opportunistic infections more likely. Cytomegalovirus is a double-stranded DNA virus of the Herpesvirus family that typically remains latent in a host after acute infection.2CMV is rarely a cause of severe disease in immunocompetent individuals. However, in immunocompromised patients such as HIV-infected patients and solid organ or hematopoietic transplant recipients, CMV can cause life-threatening, tissue-invasive disease.1,3,4In the era of antiretroviral therapy, the incidence of tissue-invasive CMV in patients with HIV is 1.2 per 1000 person-years; however, the incidence in patients with CD4 cell counts 50/mm3or less is 39 per 1000 person-years.5The most common sites of end-organ disease in HIV-infected individuals are the gastrointestinal tract (1.3 per 1000 person years) and eye (2 per 1000 person years).5In solid organ and allogeneic stem cell transplant recipients, the risk of tissue-invasive CMV infection is 3% to 10% and most frequently involves the lungs (4%) and the gastrointestinal tract (3%).4,6 CMV can affect any portion of the gastrointestinal tract but typically involves the esophagus and colon, which account for 15% and 57% of gastrointestinal tract involvement in immunocompromised hosts, respectively.7Patients with ileocolic infection may present with abdominal pain, chronic diarrhea, gastrointestinal bleeding, and perforation.7The diagnosis of tissue-invasive CMV infection requires histopathologic confirmation. Neither blood antigen testing nor whole-blood DNA polymerase chain reaction assay is sufficiently sensitive or specific to reliably diagnose CMV gastrointestinal tract disease.8 All patients with invasive CMV disease should undergo a dilated ophthalmic examination to evaluate for concomitant CMV retinitis. On ophthalmoscopic examination, CMV presents as confluent areas of retinal necrosis with hemorrhages beginning in the posterior pole and spreading centripetally. Intravenous ganciclovir is a common first-line agent to treat CMV colitis or esophagitis. If there are no concerns about intestinal absorption, oral valganciclovir is an effective alternative, based on its excellent bioavailability and noninferiority to intravenous ganciclovir in a randomized clinical trial.9Duration of therapy is 21 to 42 days or until signs and symptoms have resolved. For CMV retinitis, either intravenous ganciclovir or oral valganciclovir should be administered during an induction period lasting 14 to 21 days, with the duration determined by clinical response based on retinal examination. Induction should be followed by oral maintenance therapy with valganciclovir lasting 3 to 6 months or until immune reconstitution.1 After resection of the small intestine, the patient was treated with oral valganciclovir for 3 weeks, with no recurrence in gastrointestinal bleeding. A dilated eye examination demonstrated findings consistent with CMV retinitis, and he completed 14 days of intravenous ganciclovir followed by maintenance oral valganciclovir, with improvement in his vision. After 6 cycles of dose-adjusted R-EPOCH, a positron emission tomography scan demonstrated a complete response. He continued to receive antiretroviral therapy and had a CD4 cell count of 337/mm3at the time of last follow-up.

case_info.explanation: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis and hemorrhagic enteritis The keys to the correct diagnosis in this case are the patient’s blurred vision and gastrointestinal hemorrhage in the setting of a profound immunocompromised state. This should prompt consideration of opportunistic infectious pathogens with tropisms for the eye and gastrointestinal tract, such asToxoplasma, CMV, andCandida. The histopathologic finding of acute inflammation of the lamina propria with cytoplasmic and nuclear inclusions surrounded by a clear halo (“owl eye” sign) (Figure, left panel) confirms the diagnosis of CMV enteritis (choice C). While herpes simplex virus (choice A) is a common opportunistic infection with both ocular and gastrointestinal manifestations, it typically causes a painful keratitis and rarely involves the small or large intestines.1Vitreous fluid sampling (choice B) is occasionally indicated to evaluate for ocular involvement of lymphoma, but this procedure has associated risks and should be preceded by a thorough dilated eye examination. While Crohn disease (choice D) might present with both ocular and gastrointestinal manifestations, the patient’s age, immunocompromised state, and acute presentation make opportunistic infections more likely. Cytomegalovirus is a double-stranded DNA virus of the Herpesvirus family that typically remains latent in a host after acute infection.2CMV is rarely a cause of severe disease in immunocompetent individuals. However, in immunocompromised patients such as HIV-infected patients and solid organ or hematopoietic transplant recipients, CMV can cause life-threatening, tissue-invasive disease.1,3,4In the era of antiretroviral therapy, the incidence of tissue-invasive CMV in patients with HIV is 1.2 per 1000 person-years; however, the incidence in patients with CD4 cell counts 50/mm3or less is 39 per 1000 person-years.5The most common sites of end-organ disease in HIV-infected individuals are the gastrointestinal tract (1.3 per 1000 person years) and eye (2 per 1000 person years).5In solid organ and allogeneic stem cell transplant recipients, the risk of tissue-invasive CMV infection is 3% to 10% and most frequently involves the lungs (4%) and the gastrointestinal tract (3%).4,6 CMV can affect any portion of the gastrointestinal tract but typically involves the esophagus and colon, which account for 15% and 57% of gastrointestinal tract involvement in immunocompromised hosts, respectively.7Patients with ileocolic infection may present with abdominal pain, chronic diarrhea, gastrointestinal bleeding, and perforation.7The diagnosis of tissue-invasive CMV infection requires histopathologic confirmation. Neither blood antigen testing nor whole-blood DNA polymerase chain reaction assay is sufficiently sensitive or specific to reliably diagnose CMV gastrointestinal tract disease.8 All patients with invasive CMV disease should undergo a dilated ophthalmic examination to evaluate for concomitant CMV retinitis. On ophthalmoscopic examination, CMV presents as confluent areas of retinal necrosis with hemorrhages beginning in the posterior pole and spreading centripetally. Intravenous ganciclovir is a common first-line agent to treat CMV colitis or esophagitis. If there are no concerns about intestinal absorption, oral valganciclovir is an effective alternative, based on its excellent bioavailability and noninferiority to intravenous ganciclovir in a randomized clinical trial.9Duration of therapy is 21 to 42 days or until signs and symptoms have resolved. For CMV retinitis, either intravenous ganciclovir or oral valganciclovir should be administered during an induction period lasting 14 to 21 days, with the duration determined by clinical response based on retinal examination. Induction should be followed by oral maintenance therapy with valganciclovir lasting 3 to 6 months or until immune reconstitution.1 After resection of the small intestine, the patient was treated with oral valganciclovir for 3 weeks, with no recurrence in gastrointestinal bleeding. A dilated eye examination demonstrated findings consistent with CMV retinitis, and he completed 14 days of intravenous ganciclovir followed by maintenance oral valganciclovir, with improvement in his vision. After 6 cycles of dose-adjusted R-EPOCH, a positron emission tomography scan demonstrated a complete response. He continued to receive antiretroviral therapy and had a CD4 cell count of 337/mm3at the time of last follow-up.

A 57-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 5 months of epigastric pain and a 6.8-kg (15-lb) weight loss. He had no fevers or night sweats. Physical examination was notable for oral thrush and mild epigastric tenderness. Results of a fourth-generation HIV Ab/Ag combination assay were positive, and subsequent testing showed a CD4 cell count of 16/mm3and an HIV viral load greater than 10 million copies/mL. Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis showed thickening of the walls of the stomach, duodenum, and colon as well as multiple masses in the right hepatic lobe measuring up to 6.9 cm in diameter. A core biopsy of one of the liver masses demonstrated diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. He started antiretroviral therapy with bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir/alafenamide and chemotherapy with rituximab, etoposide, prednisone, vincristine, cyclophosphamide, and doxorubicin (R-EPOCH). Four weeks after initiation of chemotherapy, the patient developed sudden onset of bright red blood per rectum, tachycardia, and hypotension. Mesenteric computed tomography angiography demonstrated active extravasation in the jejunum from a branch of the superior mesenteric artery. After unsuccessful coil embolization, he underwent open resection of 40 cm of distal small intestine; pathological examination of a stained section showed acute inflammation of the lamina propria, with crypt epithelial apoptosis and numerous cytoplasmic and nuclear inclusions with an “owl eye” appearance (Figure 1, left panel). Five weeks later, he developed blurred vision, and visual acuity testing revealed 20/50 vision in the left eye and 20/70 in the right eye. A dilated retinal examination revealed extensive macular hemorrhage in the left eye, with peripapillary whitening and perivascular hemorrhage with whitening along the superior vascular arcade (Figure, right panel).

  A. Begin intravenous acyclovir
  B. Perform vitreal sampling for cytology and flow cytometry
  C. Begin intravenous ganciclovir
  D. Begin azathioprine and infliximab

case_info.explanation: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis and hemorrhagic enteritis The keys to the correct diagnosis in this case are the patient’s blurred vision and gastrointestinal hemorrhage in the setting of a profound immunocompromised state. This should prompt consideration of opportunistic infectious pathogens with tropisms for the eye and gastrointestinal tract, such asToxoplasma, CMV, andCandida. The histopathologic finding of acute inflammation of the lamina propria with cytoplasmic and nuclear inclusions surrounded by a clear halo (“owl eye” sign) (Figure, left panel) confirms the diagnosis of CMV enteritis (choice C). While herpes simplex virus (choice A) is a common opportunistic infection with both ocular and gastrointestinal manifestations, it typically causes a painful keratitis and rarely involves the small or large intestines.1Vitreous fluid sampling (choice B) is occasionally indicated to evaluate for ocular involvement of lymphoma, but this procedure has associated risks and should be preceded by a thorough dilated eye examination. While Crohn disease (choice D) might present with both ocular and gastrointestinal manifestations, the patient’s age, immunocompromised state, and acute presentation make opportunistic infections more likely. Cytomegalovirus is a double-stranded DNA virus of the Herpesvirus family that typically remains latent in a host after acute infection.2CMV is rarely a cause of severe disease in immunocompetent individuals. However, in immunocompromised patients such as HIV-infected patients and solid organ or hematopoietic transplant recipients, CMV can cause life-threatening, tissue-invasive disease.1,3,4In the era of antiretroviral therapy, the incidence of tissue-invasive CMV in patients with HIV is 1.2 per 1000 person-years; however, the incidence in patients with CD4 cell counts 50/mm3or less is 39 per 1000 person-years.5The most common sites of end-organ disease in HIV-infected individuals are the gastrointestinal tract (1.3 per 1000 person years) and eye (2 per 1000 person years).5In solid organ and allogeneic stem cell transplant recipients, the risk of tissue-invasive CMV infection is 3% to 10% and most frequently involves the lungs (4%) and the gastrointestinal tract (3%).4,6 CMV can affect any portion of the gastrointestinal tract but typically involves the esophagus and colon, which account for 15% and 57% of gastrointestinal tract involvement in immunocompromised hosts, respectively.7Patients with ileocolic infection may present with abdominal pain, chronic diarrhea, gastrointestinal bleeding, and perforation.7The diagnosis of tissue-invasive CMV infection requires histopathologic confirmation. Neither blood antigen testing nor whole-blood DNA polymerase chain reaction assay is sufficiently sensitive or specific to reliably diagnose CMV gastrointestinal tract disease.8 All patients with invasive CMV disease should undergo a dilated ophthalmic examination to evaluate for concomitant CMV retinitis. On ophthalmoscopic examination, CMV presents as confluent areas of retinal necrosis with hemorrhages beginning in the posterior pole and spreading centripetally. Intravenous ganciclovir is a common first-line agent to treat CMV colitis or esophagitis. If there are no concerns about intestinal absorption, oral valganciclovir is an effective alternative, based on its excellent bioavailability and noninferiority to intravenous ganciclovir in a randomized clinical trial.9Duration of therapy is 21 to 42 days or until signs and symptoms have resolved. For CMV retinitis, either intravenous ganciclovir or oral valganciclovir should be administered during an induction period lasting 14 to 21 days, with the duration determined by clinical response based on retinal examination. Induction should be followed by oral maintenance therapy with valganciclovir lasting 3 to 6 months or until immune reconstitution.1 After resection of the small intestine, the patient was treated with oral valganciclovir for 3 weeks, with no recurrence in gastrointestinal bleeding. A dilated eye examination demonstrated findings consistent with CMV retinitis, and he completed 14 days of intravenous ganciclovir followed by maintenance oral valganciclovir, with improvement in his vision. After 6 cycles of dose-adjusted R-EPOCH, a positron emission tomography scan demonstrated a complete response. He continued to receive antiretroviral therapy and had a CD4 cell count of 337/mm3at the time of last follow-up.
